opus-5.5.text:
I think the framing of "quality versus scale" is a bit of a false dichotomy, at least at this stage of embodied intelligence. In language models, we were lucky: the internet already existed, so scale came almost for free, and the hard work became filtering. In robotics, we don't have that luxury. Every trajectory costs real time, real hardware, real human effort. So the question isn't really "do I want clean data or a lot of data," it's "what is the cheapest way to get data that actually teaches the model something it couldn't learn otherwise."

The way I think about it is in layers, almost like a pyramid. At the bottom you have the very large, relatively noisy sources: internet videos of humans doing things, simulation, synthetic data from generative models. These are scalable, but the embodiment gap is big. The model sees what happens in the world, but it doesn't see the forces, the contact, the exact action that produced it. That layer is good for building priors: physics intuition, object affordances, what a "reasonable" next state looks like.

In the middle you have things like human demonstrations captured with wearable devices or low-cost teleoperation. Closer to the robot's action space, moderately scalable, moderate quality.

And at the top, you have high-quality real-robot data on the target embodiment. Expensive, small, but that's what grounds everything. You can't skip it.

So the balance, for me, is about putting each kind of data where it's most valuable rather than trying to make one source do everything. The mistake I see sometimes is people either insisting that only perfect real-robot data counts, which doesn't scale, or assuming that if you pile up enough video the robot will just figure it out, which, at least today, it doesn't.

Another thing I'd emphasize is that "quality" itself needs to be redefined. For a robot, quality isn't only about whether the demonstration is smooth or successful. Diversity matters a lot. Failure and recovery data matter a lot. A thousand perfect demonstrations of the same pick-and-place in the same lighting can be lower quality, in the sense of information content, than a hundred messy ones across varied scenes. So when we talk about data quality, I'd rather talk about coverage and informativeness than cleanliness.

And finally, I think the long-term answer is that the model has to participate in its own data collection. Once you have a reasonably capable base policy, you deploy it, it generates experience, humans intervene when needed, and those corrections are extremely high-value data. That's where scale and quality start to converge: the flywheel produces data that's both abundant and targeted at exactly what the model doesn't know yet. Getting to the point where that flywheel can actually spin is, I think, one of the most important problems in the field right now.

r001.rationale: The response says robot trajectories require real time, hardware, and human effort, and describes high-quality target-robot data as expensive and small, explaining why embodied data is harder to scale.

r002.rationale: The response proposes prioritizing coverage and informativeness and assigning different data sources different roles. It does not state that it remains unclear which quality requirements can be relaxed for more volume.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the premise that you have to trade one off against the other is a bit of a trap, and it comes from importing intuitions from language models too directly.

In language, "scale" was almost free. The internet already existed, it was already text, and the main job was filtering. So the question became: how much do you clean versus how much do you keep? For embodied intelligence, that's not the situation at all. There is no internet of robot trajectories. Every piece of data costs money, costs time, and involves a physical body moving in the real world. So when people say "we need scale," they're often not saying something about the data itself. They're saying something about how badly they want the language-model story to repeat.

My view is that quality and scale are answers to two different questions. Quality determines the ceiling of what the model can learn from a given distribution. Scale determines how broad the distribution is. And in robotics, the problem that kills you is almost never that your demonstrations are a little noisy. It's that the model has never seen anything like the situation it's in. The cup is a slightly different shape, the lighting changed, the table is three centimeters higher. So if I have to choose, I'd choose diversity over polish every time. A hundred thousand slightly imperfect episodes across many objects and scenes teach the model more than ten thousand beautiful ones from a single lab setup.

But there's a subtlety. "Imperfect" is not the same as "wrong." Low-quality data in the sense of jittery teleoperation or a hesitant operator is fine, and sometimes even useful, because the model learns to recover. Low-quality data in the sense of mislabeled tasks, broken timing between vision and action, or demonstrations that accomplish the goal by accident — that's poison, and it doesn't get averaged out by scale. It actively teaches the wrong thing. So the quality bar I care about is consistency and correctness of the signal, not smoothness of the motion.

The second thing is that in embodied AI, you can't separate the data question from the source question. Where does the data come from? Real-robot teleoperation is the gold standard but it's the slowest. Simulation scales beautifully but has the gap problem. Human video is enormous and diverse but has the embodiment gap. I don't think any single one of these wins. The practical answer is that you use the cheap, large sources to learn the general structure of the world — what objects are, how things move, what a reasonable sequence of actions looks like — and you use the expensive, high-quality robot data to ground that into actual control. The expensive data is doing alignment, not pretraining, if you want to borrow the language.

And if you look at it that way, the quality-versus-scale question dissolves into an allocation question. You want the biggest possible net for the layers of the problem that are cheap to cover, and you want very deliberate, very clean data for the narrow layer where the model has to actually commit to a motor command. Spending your limited high-quality budget trying to achieve scale is a mistake. Spending your scalable sources trying to achieve precision is also a mistake.

The last thing I'd say is that the real bottleneck right now isn't really either of these. It's evaluation. In language we could argue about data forever because we could measure the result cheaply. In robotics, to know whether your data strategy worked, you have to run a robot, in a real environment, many times. That's slow and noisy. So a lot of the debate about quality and scale is happening in the absence of good feedback. I suspect once evaluation becomes cheaper — through better sim, through standardized real-world benchmarks — a lot of these arguments will resolve themselves pretty quickly, and we'll find out that some of the things we were religious about didn't matter and some things we ignored mattered a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says robot trajectories must be collected through costly, time-consuming physical interaction and that there is no ready-made internet-scale source, explaining why embodied data are harder to scale.

r002.rationale: The response gives a clear view of what can be relaxed (motion smoothness) and what cannot (signal correctness and consistency); it does not say the tradeoff remains unclear.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to ask what you want the data to teach the model. For embodied intelligence, more data is useful only if it adds something: a new environment, a new interaction, or a way to recover when an action goes wrong. Repeating the same successful behavior many times can increase the dataset size without making the system much more capable.

So I would start with a carefully checked dataset to establish the behaviors we care about, then expand collection around the model’s weaknesses. Where does it fail? Which objects or situations does it struggle with? Those failures help determine what to collect next.

Quality also doesn’t necessarily mean keeping only perfect demonstrations. A failed attempt can be valuable if we can understand what happened and whether the robot recovered. What matters is that the observations, actions, and outcomes are reliable enough to learn from.

Ultimately, I’d judge the balance by performance in unfamiliar situations, rather than by dataset size alone. You need a loop between collecting data, training the model, and testing it. That loop is what makes scaling productive.

r001.rationale: The response discusses collecting useful data at scale, but does not say that embodied-intelligence data’s more demanding requirements make it harder to scale.

r002.rationale: The response does not address whether any data-quality requirements can be relaxed in exchange for greater volume, or say that this remains unclear.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to ask what we want to scale. For embodied intelligence, collecting more hours of data doesn’t necessarily mean collecting more useful experience. If the robot repeats the same successful motion in the same environment, the dataset grows, but its coverage may not improve very much.

So I would start with a smaller, carefully controlled dataset to establish that the model can learn the behavior we care about. Then, as we scale, we should expand the diversity of tasks, environments, objects, and interactions, while maintaining a consistent standard for the data. Quality also doesn’t mean keeping only perfect demonstrations. Failures and recovery behaviors can be valuable, provided we can understand what happened.

The important thing is to close the loop between data collection and evaluation. Where does the model fail? Is it missing a particular skill, or does it struggle when the environment changes? Those answers should guide the next round of collection. In that sense, quality and scalability are not separate goals. A good data pipeline makes it possible to scale useful experience, rather than simply scale volume.

r001.rationale: The response says that simply collecting more hours may add little coverage and recommends diverse data, but it does not explain that more demanding training-data requirements make scaling harder.

r002.rationale: The response recommends maintaining a consistent data standard; it does not say that it remains unclear which quality requirements could be relaxed to increase data volume.
